variants.note: the strong form, the same sound as the name of the letter a, used when the word is stressed or said alone

pronunciation.notes: A is normally unstressed, ə, before a consonant sound (a book, a university). Before a vowel sound, an is used instead (an apple). The strong form, eɪ, is used when the word is stressed or said alone.

core_idea: A introduces a person or thing as one example of its kind, without pointing to a particular, already-known one.

senses.definition: used before a singular countable noun to talk about a person or thing without saying which one, especially the first time it is mentioned
senses.explanation: The listener does not yet know which one is meant, or it does not matter which: I saw a bird in the garden. Once something has been introduced this way, the usually takes over the next time it is mentioned: I saw a bird in the garden; the bird was blue.

examples.text: I saw a bird in the garden this morning.
Would you like a cup of tea?
She works as a teacher at a school near here.
There's a message for you on the table.

compare.note: the is used instead once the listener already knows which one is meant
an is used instead of a directly before a vowel sound

senses.definition: used before a singular countable noun to make a general statement about every member of a kind
senses.explanation: This use talks about the whole kind, not one particular example: a triangle has three sides means every triangle. It often follows a form of be or have.

examples.text: A good teacher listens to students.
A computer needs electricity to run.
A cat is a very independent animal.

senses.definition: used after a number or amount and before a noun of time or measurement to mean each or every
senses.explanation: This use gives a rate: how often, how much, or how fast something happens: three times a week, twenty dollars a ticket.

examples.text: Sam goes to the gym three times a week.
The tickets cost twenty dollars a person.
We meet once a month to talk about the project.

synonym_discrimination.note: A and an are the same word; the choice depends only on the sound that follows, not the spelling: a before a consonant sound (a car, a university, a one-way street), an before a vowel sound (an apple, an hour, an MP).

usage_note: A and an have no plural. Where the same idea is needed before a plural or uncountable noun, some, any, or no article at all is used instead: a book, but some books; a piece of advice, but some advice.

learner_errors.note: A singular countable noun after be needs a determiner; many languages allow no article here.
An is wrongly used before new, which begins with a consonant sound.

learner_errors.incorrect: I have a advice for you.
learner_errors.correct: I have some advice for you.
learner_errors.note: Advice is uncountable and never follows a; use some or a piece of advice.

adaptation.grammar: A singular countable noun in English almost always needs a or an, or another determiner; learners from languages with no articles often leave it out.
adaptation.pronunciation: A is normally unstressed, ə; the strong form eɪ, the same sound as the name of the letter a, is used only when the word is stressed or said alone.
